title: Functions & Multiple Return Values
summary: A **function** in Go is a named, reusable block of code with typed parameters and typed results. Go's standout traits are **multiple return values** — powering the idiomatic `(result, error)` pattern — plus strict **pass-by-value** semantics, **variadic** parameters, and **first-class** functions that you can pass around and close over.

subtopics.title: Declaration & parameters
subtopics.explanation: A function is declared with func name(params) results { ... }. Parameters list a name then a type; consecutive same-typed params can share the type (a, b int). Every parameter is a typed local variable initialized from the caller's argument.
subtopics.example: func add(a, b int) int { return a + b }

subtopics.title: Pass-by-value
subtopics.explanation: Go always copies arguments into the parameters. For ints/structs the callee gets an independent copy. For slices, maps, and pointers the *header/reference* is copied, so the callee can mutate the shared underlying data even though it can't reassign the caller's variable.
subtopics.example: func bump(s []int) { s[0]++ } // caller's element changes

subtopics.title: Multiple return values
subtopics.explanation: A function can return several values: func divmod(a, b int) (int, int). The caller destructures them with q, r := divmod(7, 3). This is how Go returns a result alongside an error without exceptions.

subtopics.title: The (result, error) pattern
subtopics.explanation: The dominant idiom: return your value plus an error, and the caller checks err first. A non-nil error means the result is usually the zero value and should be ignored.
subtopics.example: v, err := strconv.Atoi(s); if err != nil { return err }

subtopics.title: Named returns & naked return
subtopics.explanation: You can name result values (func f() (n int, err error)); they become zero-valued locals you can assign, and a bare return sends their current values. Handy with defer, but naked returns hurt readability in long functions and are discouraged there.
subtopics.example: func f() (n int, err error) { n = 42; return }

subtopics.title: Variadic functions
subtopics.explanation: A trailing ...T parameter accepts any number of args, received as a []T slice. Spread an existing slice into it with slice... . fmt.Println and append are variadic.

foundations.overview: Functions are how you name, reuse, and compose behavior in Go. Two design choices make Go functions distinctive: they can return more than one value, and they are passed strictly by value. Multiple returns give Go its signature (result, error) idiom — error handling as ordinary values rather than exceptions. Pass-by-value means every argument is copied; understanding what exactly gets copied (a whole struct vs. a slice header) is the key to reasoning about whether a function can change your data.
foundations.formalDefinition: A function is a named (or anonymous) sequence of statements with a typed parameter list and a typed, possibly multi-value result list; it is a first-class value of a function type and is invoked by copying arguments into fresh parameters.
foundations.whyItMatters: Functions are the unit of reuse and the building block of every Go program. The (result, error) convention shapes how all idiomatic Go handles failure, and pass-by-value semantics are one of the most common interview topics and a frequent source of beginner confusion.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a function as a vending machine: you feed in copies of your inputs (the machine never reaches back into your pocket), it runs its process, and it can drop out more than one item at once — a value and a little receipt (the error) telling you whether it worked.
foundations.runtimePerspective: On a call, Go evaluates the arguments, copies them onto the new call's stack frame, and runs the body. Multiple return values are placed where the caller expects them. When the function returns, any deferred calls run in LIFO order, then the frame is reclaimed. Small functions are often inlined by the compiler, erasing the call overhead entirely.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Every standard-library API uses these patterns: os.Open returns (*os.File, error); strconv.Atoi returns (int, error); fmt.Println is variadic; http.HandlerFunc shows functions as first-class values; closures capture per-request state in handlers.
foundations.businessImpact: Consistent (result, error) handling makes failures explicit and auditable, reducing silent data corruption and outages — errors are values you must deal with, not hidden control flow.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Clear parameter and return types make functions self-documenting; first-class functions and closures enable clean dependency injection and middleware without heavy frameworks.
foundations.performanceImpact: Copying small values is cheap and stack-friendly; copying large structs by value can cost — pass a pointer instead. Inlining removes call overhead for tiny helpers, and avoiding accidental heap escapes (via closures) keeps allocation low.
commonUseCases: Returning (value, error) from any fallible operation
Closures capturing state for callbacks and middleware
defer Close() / defer Unlock() for guaranteed cleanup

commonMisconceptions.myth: Passing a slice or map to a function copies all its data.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only the small header/reference is copied. The callee shares the same underlying array/map, so it can mutate elements — it just can't grow the caller's slice via append.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Go has pass-by-reference for some types.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Go is always pass-by-value. Slices, maps, and pointers feel like references only because the value being copied is itself a reference-like header or address.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Naked returns are good Go style.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Named results are fine, but a bare `return` far from where the names were set hurts readability; explicit `return a, b` is preferred in non-trivial functions.

visualExplorer.title: Anatomy of a function call
visualExplorer.caption: What the runtime does from the moment you call a function until it returns its values.

config.intro: Calling `q, err := divide(a, b)` step by step:

steps.name: Evaluate arguments
steps.detail: The caller evaluates each argument expression (a, b) to a value before the call happens.

steps.name: Copy into parameters
steps.detail: Those values are COPIED into fresh parameter variables on the new stack frame — the callee can't touch the caller's variables (only shared data behind a slice/map/pointer).

steps.name: Run the body
steps.detail: The function executes; named results, if any, start at their zero values and can be assigned along the way.

steps.name: Place return values
steps.detail: A `return` (or naked `return`) hands the result list back to the spot the caller is waiting on.

steps.name: Run deferred calls (LIFO)
steps.detail: Any `defer`red calls run in last-in-first-out order — after the results are set but before control truly leaves.

steps.name: Reclaim the frame
steps.detail: The stack frame is freed and the caller resumes with the returned values destructured into q and err.

interactiveExamples.title: Multiple returns and the (result, error) pattern
interactiveExamples.explanation: divide returns two values: the quotient and an error. The caller checks err first; only when err is nil is the result trustworthy. Returning errors as values is the heart of idiomatic Go.

interactiveExamples.title: Pass-by-value: what a function can and can't change
interactiveExamples.explanation: An int is copied, so doubling it inside a function never touches the caller's variable. A slice header is also copied, but it points at the SAME backing array, so mutating an element IS visible to the caller.

code.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func doubleVal(n int)   { n = n * 2 }     // copy of the int; caller unaffected
func bumpFirst(s []int) { s[0] = s[0] + 100 } // shares the backing array

func main() {
	x := 5
	doubleVal(x)
	fmt.Println("x after doubleVal:", x) // still 5

	nums := []int{1, 2, 3}
	bumpFirst(nums)
	fmt.Println("nums after bumpFirst:", nums) // [101 2 3]
}
code.expectedOutput:
x after doubleVal: 5
nums after bumpFirst: [101 2 3]

checkpoints.prompt: You call `func grow(s []int) { s = append(s, 9) }` then print the caller's slice. Why is the appended 9 usually NOT visible to the caller?
options: append is not allowed inside functions
The function receives a COPY of the slice header; reassigning it (via append's result) doesn't change the caller's header
Go passes slices by reference, so it should be visible
checkpoints.explanation: Go copies the slice header into the parameter. append returns a new header (possibly a new array) that is assigned to the local copy only — the caller's header is untouched. To propagate growth, return the slice: s = grow(s).

checkpoints.prompt: This is meant to return the value and report 'not found'. What's wrong?
options: It never reports a missing key — it should use the comma-ok form to detect absence
error must come before the int
checkpoints.explanation: Indexing a missing key returns the zero value (0) with no signal, so a real 0 and a missing key look identical. Use the comma-ok idiom: v, ok := m[k]; if !ok { return 0, errors.New("not found") }.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the call so the slice's elements are passed as individual variadic arguments.
checkpoints.explanation: The spread operator goes AFTER the slice: sum(xs...). Passing xs without ... is a type error (a []int where ...int args are expected), and ...xs is invalid syntax.

debuggingLab.title: The error is always nil
debuggingLab.symptom: parse() never reports failures even when Atoi clearly fails — err is always nil at the return.

brokenCode.caption: This won't even compile, which hints at the real problem.

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Using `:=` with named results re-declares NEW local variables n and err that SHADOW the named results, so the values you compute never reach the ones being returned. In practice the compiler flags 'no new variables on left side of :=' (both names already exist), which is the tell that you meant assignment.
commonMistakes: Using := instead of = when result variables are already named.
Accidentally shadowing err inside an if/for block so the outer err stays nil.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Assign to the existing named results with = (or drop the names and return strconv.Atoi(s) directly).

solution.expectedOutput:
parse("42") -> 42, <nil>
parse("x")  -> 0, strconv.Atoi: parsing "x": invalid syntax

theory.question: Is Go pass-by-value or pass-by-reference? Why can a function still modify a slice's contents?
theory.directAnswer: Go is always pass-by-value: every argument is copied into the parameter. A function can still change a slice's elements because what gets copied is the slice header (pointer, length, capacity) — and that copied pointer still points at the same backing array. It cannot, however, change the caller's header (e.g. make it longer via append) since that's a separate copy.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The argument-passing semantics of Go: copy the value into the parameter.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Pass-by-value is simple and predictable; reference-like behavior is achieved explicitly via pointers, slices, and maps rather than hidden language magic.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Scalars and structs copy their full contents; slices/maps/pointers copy a small header or address that aliases shared underlying data.

theory.whyImportant: Misunderstanding this causes both 'why didn't my change stick?' and 'why did the caller's data change unexpectedly?' bugs — a classic interview probe.
theory.realWorldExample: Passing a large config struct by value copies it entirely (costly); passing *Config copies only an 8-byte pointer and lets the callee mutate it.

followUps.question: How do you let a function modify a caller's int?
followUps.answer: Pass a pointer (*int) and dereference: *p = newVal. The pointer is copied, but it still addresses the caller's variable.

followUps.question: Why can't append inside a function grow the caller's slice?
followUps.answer: append may allocate a new array and returns a new header assigned only to the local copy; the caller's header is unchanged unless you return and reassign it.

theory.question: What are named return values and naked returns, and when should you avoid them?
theory.directAnswer: Named returns declare the result variables in the signature (func f() (n int, err error)); they start at their zero values, can be assigned in the body, and a bare `return` returns their current values. They read well in short functions and pair nicely with defer that sets the error, but in long functions a naked return forces the reader to scan back for what's being returned, so explicit `return a, b` is preferred there.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Result parameters that are named in the signature and behave like pre-declared local variables.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To document what each result means and to let deferred functions inspect or modify the results (e.g. wrap an error).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The names are zero-valued at entry; `return` with no operands ('naked') returns whatever they currently hold.

theory.whyImportant: Knowing the trade-off shows idiomatic judgment; misuse (shadowing or distant naked returns) is a common readability and correctness pitfall.
theory.realWorldExample: func read() (data []byte, err error) { defer func(){ if err != nil { err = fmt.Errorf("read: %w", err) } }(); ... } — defer wraps the named err.

followUps.question: Can a deferred function change the returned value?
followUps.answer: Yes — if results are named, a deferred closure can modify them after the return statement runs but before the caller receives them.

scenario.question: A teammate's function returns (data, err) but callers keep using data even when err != nil, occasionally processing garbage. How should the API and callers be structured?
scenario.directAnswer: Follow the Go convention: on error, return the zero value for data and a non-nil error, and require callers to check err FIRST and return/handle before touching data. Document that data is only valid when err == nil. Callers should write `data, err := f(); if err != nil { return err }` rather than using data unconditionally.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The (result, error) contract: the result is meaningful only when error is nil.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go has no exceptions; errors are ordinary return values, so the discipline of checking them is what keeps programs correct.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Functions return zero + error on failure; the idiom `if err != nil { ... }` immediately after the call enforces handling.

scenario.whyImportant: Ignoring errors and using partial results is a leading cause of subtle data-corruption bugs in Go services.
scenario.realWorldExample: json.Unmarshal returns an error; using the half-filled struct on error leads to processing malformed records.

followUps.question: How can the linter help enforce this?
followUps.answer: errcheck (and go vet via some analyzers) flags ignored error return values, catching `data, _ := f()` style mistakes.

coding.question: Implement `func Map(xs []int, f func(int) int) []int` that returns a new slice with f applied to each element.
coding.thoughtProcess: f is a first-class function value passed as a parameter, so we just call it per element. Pre-size the result to len(xs) to avoid reallocations, then apply f to each input and write it into the output. This is the classic higher-order map.
coding.lineByLine: We allocate out with the same length as xs so no growth happens. We range over xs getting index and value, call the passed function f on each value, and store the transformed result at the matching index. The function parameter f demonstrates functions as first-class values. Finally we return the new, independent slice.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) — one call to f per element.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the output slice (input is left unchanged).

followUps.question: How would you make Map generic over any type?
followUps.answer: Use type parameters: func Map[T, U any](xs []T, f func(T) U) []U, available since Go 1.18.

followUps.question: Could you pass a closure as f?
followUps.answer: Yes — e.g. factor := 3; Map(xs, func(x int) int { return x * factor }) captures factor by reference.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Design function signatures as contracts: return (T, error) for anything fallible, accept interfaces and small structs, and prefer pure functions where possible for testability. Use functional options (...Option) for extensible constructors.
productionDeepDive.performance: Pass large structs by pointer to avoid expensive copies, but keep small values on the stack for cheap, GC-free calls. Watch for closures and interface conversions that force values to escape to the heap; check with `go build -gcflags=-m`.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: A function that mutates data shared via a captured variable or slice header is not automatically safe across goroutines — guard shared state with a mutex or pass copies. Be careful that closures launched in goroutines capture the intended values.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Use defer for guaranteed cleanup (defer f.Close(), defer mu.Unlock()) so resources are released on every return path, including panics. Return wrapped errors (fmt.Errorf with %w) so callers can inspect the cause.
productionDeepDive.observability: Standardize error wrapping at function boundaries so logs and traces carry context (operation name, key inputs). Consistent (result, error) signatures make instrumentation and middleware uniform.
productionDeepDive.security: Validate inputs at the function boundary and never assume a result is valid when err != nil. Avoid leaking sensitive arguments through error strings or logs.

caseStudies.solution: Pervasive (result, error) return signatures, e.g. os.Open, strconv.Atoi, net.Dial.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: More boilerplate `if err != nil` checks, but errors are explicit and never silently swallowed.
caseStudies.lessons: Returning errors as values makes failure paths visible and forces conscious handling.

caseStudies.problem: Inconsistent constructors with many optional parameters.
caseStudies.solution: The functional-options pattern using variadic ...Option functions that close over configuration.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly more code than positional args, but extensible and backward-compatible.
caseStudies.lessons: First-class functions and variadics combine into clean, evolvable APIs.

keyTakeaways: Go is always pass-by-value: arguments are copied; slices/maps/pointers copy a header/address that still aliases shared data, so callees can mutate contents but not the caller's variable.
Multiple return values power the idiomatic (result, error) pattern — check the error first and treat the result as valid only when err is nil.
Named results and naked returns are convenient (especially with defer) but hurt readability in long functions; prefer explicit returns there, and avoid shadowing with :=.
Variadic ...T collects args into a slice (spread with slice...), and functions are first-class values that closures can capture by reference; defer runs deferred calls LIFO at return.
